title: Progressives and Empire
bigQuestion: When Americans decided that the problems of the industrial age needed fixing, why did some reach for reform at home and others for power abroad, and were those the same impulse?

story.title: A House on Halsted Street
story.kicker: In September 1889 two young women from small-town Illinois moved into a run-down mansion in the middle of Chicago's immigrant West Side and invited the neighbors in.
paragraphs: Jane Addams was twenty-eight, the daughter of a wealthy mill owner and state senator from Cedarville, in the far north of Illinois. She had a college degree, which was rare, and no clear use for it, which was common. Women of her class were expected to marry or to stay home with their families. For most of her twenties she had drifted, ill and unhappy, through Europe. In London she visited Toynbee Hall, where university men lived among the poor of the East End and tried to be good neighbors. She came home with a plan.

With her friend Ellen Gates Starr, she rented the second floor of an old house built by a real estate man named Charles Hull. It stood at Halsted and Polk streets, in a neighborhood packed with Italians, Greeks, Russian Jews, Bohemians and Irish, where the streets were unpaved, garbage rotted in wooden boxes and children worked in sweatshops. They called it Hull House. The idea was simple and, for the time, strange: educated women would live there, not visit, and find out what the neighborhood needed by asking.

What it needed, it turned out, was almost everything. Within a few years Hull House ran a kindergarten, a day nursery for the children of working mothers, English classes, a gymnasium, a public bath, a coffee house, an art gallery, a labor museum and a meeting hall used by unions and immigrant societies. Addams got herself appointed garbage inspector for the ward so she could follow the collection wagons at six in the morning and report the ones that skipped streets.

The residents also counted. In 1895 they published Hull-House Maps and Papers, a block-by-block survey of the neighborhood showing who lived where, what they earned and where they came from. Florence Kelley, a resident, used her research on sweatshops to push through Illinois's 1893 factory law, which limited women's hours and barred children under fourteen from factory work; the state then hired her as its first chief factory inspector. Other residents helped create the first juvenile court in the country, in Cook County in 1899.

Hull House became the model for hundreds of settlement houses across the country, and Addams became one of the most famous women in America. She campaigned for suffrage, for peace during the First World War, when newspapers turned on her, and for the rights of immigrants. In 1931 she became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her method, go and look, count and ask, then organize, is the method of the Progressive era in one house. The house still stands on Halsted Street, in the middle of a university campus.
story.think: Addams insisted that Hull House helped her and Starr as much as it helped the neighborhood. What might she have meant, and does it change how you judge the work?

lessons.title: Muckrakers and the Jungle
lessons.mainIdea: Investigative journalists exposed corruption and dangerous products to a mass readership, and public outrage forced Congress to act.
reading: In 1904 a young socialist writer named Upton Sinclair spent seven weeks in Chicago's Packingtown, walking through the plants in workman's clothes and talking to the families who lived in the shadow of the stockyards. His novel The Jungle, published in 1906, followed a Lithuanian immigrant family through injury, fraud, hunger and death. He meant it as an argument for socialism. What readers noticed were the chapters on meat: diseased cattle sold as beef, rats and sawdust swept into sausage, workers who fell into rendering vats.

Sinclair later said he had aimed at the public's heart and hit it in the stomach. Within months, Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the *Pure Food and Drug Act* of 1906, requiring federal inspection of packing plants and honest labels on food and medicine. Patent medicines that had been sold as cures for everything, some laced with alcohol, opium or cocaine, now had to list their ingredients. The packers themselves supported inspection, since European buyers had stopped trusting American meat.

Sinclair was one of a group of writers Theodore Roosevelt called *muckrakers*, after a character in an old story who was so busy raking filth that he never looked up. Roosevelt meant it as a partial insult; the writers wore it with pride. Ida Tarbell, whose father had been ruined by Standard Oil, spent five years in company records and published a history of the company in McClure's Magazine that laid out the rebates and threats in detail. Lincoln Steffens traced bribery in city after city, including Chicago, in The Shame of the Cities.

What made muckraking possible was a new kind of magazine. Cheap paper, photographs and national advertising let McClure's and its rivals sell for ten or fifteen cents and reach hundreds of thousands of middle-class readers. Those readers, many of them women who could not yet vote, wrote letters, joined clubs and pressed legislators. The pattern, investigate, publish, organize, legislate, became the standard method of the *Progressive* movement, the broad effort between about 1890 and 1920 to use government to fix the problems of the industrial age.

words.d: a journalist of the early 1900s who investigated and exposed corruption, fraud or dangerous conditions
the 1906 federal law requiring honest labels and banning harmful or mislabeled food and medicine
a reformer of the years around 1890 to 1920 who believed government should solve the problems of industrial society
a remedy sold with secret ingredients and bold claims, often containing alcohol or drugs

look.title: What Went Into the Sausage
look.text: Sinclair described meat that had fallen on the floor, where workers spat and rats ran, being swept into the hoppers along with the poisoned bread set out for the rats, and all of it going into sausage that was sold as fresh.
look.prompt: Sinclair wanted readers to care about the workers. Why do you think they cared more about the sausage, and what does that tell reformers about how to win?

check.q: What did the Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 require?
choices: Federal inspection of packing plants and honest labeling of food and medicine
A ban on all imported meat
Government ownership of the stockyards
Higher wages for packinghouse workers
check.why: Both laws responded to The Jungle by putting federal inspectors in plants and requiring truthful labels.

check.q: Why did Roosevelt's word muckraker have a mixed meaning?
choices: It was the name of a magazine
He meant it as a criticism, but the writers adopted it with pride
It described only photographers
It was a compliment that writers rejected
check.why: Roosevelt implied the writers never looked up from the filth, but they took the label as a badge of honor.

check.q: Which change most enabled muckraking to reach a mass audience?
choices: Free public libraries
Radio broadcasts
Cheap magazines with photographs and national advertising
Government printing offices
check.why: Ten-cent magazines like McClure's put investigative reporting in front of hundreds of thousands of readers.

lessons.title: Children in the Mills
lessons.mainIdea: Progressives fought child labor with photographs, state laws and a federal law the Supreme Court struck down, and the fight was not finished for another generation.
reading: In 1900 the census counted about 1.75 million children between ten and fifteen at work, roughly one in six, and the true number was higher because many were younger than ten. Boys sorted coal in Pennsylvania breakers, breathing dust for ten hours a day. Girls tended spinning frames in Southern cotton mills, some so small they stood on boxes. In Chicago, children rolled cigars in tenement rooms and delivered messages at night. Families needed the wages; a father's pay in a packinghouse often could not feed a household alone.

The most effective weapon against child labor was a camera. Lewis Hine, a schoolteacher, took a job as an investigator for the National Child Labor Committee in 1908 and spent years photographing children at work, often sneaking into factories by claiming to be a postcard salesman. He measured children against his coat buttons to record their height and wrote down their names and ages. The pictures, of a barefoot girl in a mill, of a newsboy asleep on a stoop, appeared in magazines and exhibits across the country.

Illinois had led with its 1893 factory law barring children under fourteen, though enforcement was weak and the Illinois Supreme Court struck down the law's limit on women's hours in 1895. In 1916 Congress passed the Keating-Owen Act, barring goods made by child labor from interstate commerce. Two years later, in Hammer v. Dagenhart, the Supreme Court struck it down, ruling that Congress could regulate commerce but not manufacturing, which belonged to the states. A second attempt using the tax power also failed. Federal child labor limits did not survive in court until 1941.

The wider problem was the workplace itself. In March 1911 a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist factory in New York killed 146 garment workers, most of them young immigrant women, because the owners kept a stairway door locked to prevent theft. Many jumped from the ninth floor. The state responded with the strongest factory safety laws in the country. A young factory inspector named Frances Perkins watched the fire from the street; twenty-two years later she became the first woman in a president's cabinet and helped write the law that finally ended child labor.

words.d: the employment of children, common in mines, mills and street trades around 1900
the 1916 federal law against child labor that the Supreme Court struck down in 1918
the 1918 Supreme Court case ruling that Congress could not use its commerce power to regulate child labor in factories
the 1911 New York garment factory fire that killed 146 workers and led to new safety laws

look.title: Reading a Photograph
look.text: Imagine one of Lewis Hine's photographs from about 1909. A girl of perhaps ten stands in a cotton mill between two rows of spinning frames taller than she is. Her feet are bare on the oily floor. She looks straight at the camera. On the back, Hine has written her height, her name, and the words: has been working a year, sometimes at night.
look.prompt: Why did Hine record the names, heights and ages so carefully? What might a mill owner say the photograph leaves out, and how would you answer?

check.q: Why did many families send children to work, according to the lesson?
choices: Children preferred factories to school
Laws required it
There were no schools in cities
A single adult wage often could not support a household
check.why: Low adult wages meant families depended on children's earnings to eat and pay rent.

check.q: On what grounds did the Supreme Court strike down the Keating-Owen Act?
choices: Congress could regulate interstate commerce but not manufacturing inside a state
Children had a right to work
The law was too expensive
The states had already banned child labor
check.why: Hammer v. Dagenhart drew a line between commerce, which Congress could regulate, and production, which it said belonged to the states.

check.q: What did the Triangle fire reveal about factory conditions?
choices: That fire drills were common
That locked exits and lack of safety rules could turn a fire into mass death
That garment work was mostly done by men
That New York had no factories
check.why: A locked stairway door and no working escape routes trapped 146 workers, prompting sweeping state safety laws.

lessons.title: The Long Road to Suffrage
lessons.mainIdea: Women won the vote state by state and then by constitutional amendment, using patient lobbying, mass parades and civil disobedience, and Illinois was an early turning point.
reading: When the Civil War ended, women who had fought against slavery expected the vote alongside Black men. The Fifteenth Amendment left them out, and the movement split over whether to support it. For decades the *suffragists* worked state by state. Wyoming Territory let women vote in 1869, and by 1896 Colorado, Utah and Idaho had followed, but every eastern state said no. Opponents, including many women, argued that politics would coarsen women and that the home, not the ballot box, was their sphere of influence.

The new century brought new tactics. The National American Woman Suffrage Association, led after 1915 by Carrie Chapman Catt, ran a disciplined campaign in every state and in Congress at once. In 1913 Illinois became the first state east of the Mississippi to give women the vote for president and local offices, a law that suffragists across the country cited as proof that a big industrial state could be won. Chicago's Black women's clubs, led by Ida B. Wells, organized the Alpha Suffrage Club the same year and helped elect the city's first Black alderman in 1915.

Alice Paul, a young Quaker who had learned militant tactics in Britain, thought lobbying was too slow. Her National Woman's Party organized a parade of thousands in Washington the day before Woodrow Wilson's inauguration in 1913; crowds attacked the marchers while police stood by. In 1917 her Silent Sentinels picketed the White House with banners asking how long women must wait for liberty. Arrested, jailed and force-fed when they went on hunger strike, they made the government look cruel and the cause urgent.

The First World War tipped the balance. Women filled jobs in factories, drove ambulances and sold war bonds, and Wilson finally endorsed the amendment in 1918 as a war measure. Congress passed it in June 1919, and Illinois ratified it on June 10, one of the first states to act. Tennessee provided the thirty-sixth ratification in August 1920 by a single vote, after a young legislator changed his mind on his mother's advice. The *Nineteenth Amendment* was the largest single expansion of the electorate in American history. In the South, Black women, like Black men, would still be turned away for decades.

words.d: a person who campaigned for women's right to vote
the 1920 constitutional amendment barring states from denying the vote on account of sex
to formally approve; three-fourths of the states must ratify an amendment
deliberately breaking a law or rule in public to protest an injustice

look.title: The Amendment's Words
look.text: The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.
look.cite: Nineteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified 1920
look.prompt: Compare this wording to the Fifteenth Amendment, which bars denying the vote on account of race. Why could both be in the Constitution while Black women in the South still could not vote?

check.q: Why was Illinois's 1913 suffrage law important beyond Illinois?
choices: It was the first suffrage law anywhere
It gave women the vote in all elections
It showed a large eastern industrial state could be won, encouraging campaigns elsewhere
It was written by Alice Paul
check.why: Illinois was the first state east of the Mississippi to grant women presidential suffrage, a breakthrough suffragists used as an argument.

check.q: How did Alice Paul's tactics differ from Carrie Chapman Catt's?
choices: Paul worked only in the West
Paul opposed the federal amendment
Paul refused to speak in public
Paul used parades, pickets and jail to pressure the president, while Catt ran organized lobbying campaigns
check.why: The National Woman's Party used confrontation and civil disobedience; NAWSA relied on disciplined state and congressional campaigns.

check.q: Why did the Nineteenth Amendment not guarantee the vote to Black women in the South?
choices: Southern states used the same poll taxes, literacy tests and violence that already kept Black men from voting
The amendment applied only to white women
Black women were not citizens
Southern states refused to ratify it
check.why: The amendment barred denial on account of sex, but the tools of disfranchisement by race remained in place.

lessons.title: Roosevelt and the Square Deal
lessons.mainIdea: Theodore Roosevelt made the presidency an active force, breaking a railroad trust, settling a coal strike and protecting vast public lands.
reading: Theodore Roosevelt became president in September 1901 when an anarchist shot William McKinley. He was forty-two, the youngest president ever, a former New York police commissioner, rancher, war hero and governor who had been put on the ticket to get him out of the way. Within months he showed what he meant to do. In 1902 his Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company, a railroad combination put together by J. P. Morgan, under the Sherman Act. Morgan came to the White House to ask if they could fix it up. Roosevelt said no. In 1904 the Supreme Court ordered the company dissolved.

That same year, 1902, about 140,000 Pennsylvania coal miners struck for higher pay and an eight-hour day. As winter approached, coal prices soared and cities faced cold. The mine owners refused to talk to the union. Roosevelt summoned both sides to the White House, the first time a president had treated a union as an equal party, and threatened to send the army to run the mines. The owners agreed to *arbitration*, and the miners won a raise and shorter hours. Roosevelt called it a *square deal* for everyone, and the phrase became his slogan.

Roosevelt did not oppose big business as such. He distinguished good trusts, which were efficient and behaved, from bad ones that cheated, and he preferred regulation to breaking companies up. He signed the Hepburn Act in 1906, giving the Interstate Commerce Commission real power to set railroad rates, and the food and drug laws of the same year. He believed a strong national government was the only force that could stand up to national corporations. Critics on the right called him a socialist; socialists called him a fraud.

His most lasting work was *conservation*. A lifelong outdoorsman who had watched the buffalo disappear, he used the power to set aside public land more than any president before him: about 230 million acres of national forests, parks, monuments and wildlife refuges, an area larger than Texas. With Gifford Pinchot, the first head of the U.S. Forest Service in 1905, he argued that forests and rivers should be managed for long-term public use, not sold off for quick profit. John Muir, who wanted wilderness left untouched, thought Pinchot's approach did not go far enough. That argument continues.

words.d: Roosevelt's promise that government would treat business, labor and the public fairly
settling a dispute by letting a neutral third party decide the terms
managing forests, water and land so that they last for future generations
using the Sherman Act to break up business combinations judged to be harmful

look.title: Larger Than Texas
look.text: Between 1901 and 1909 Roosevelt set aside about 230 million acres of national forests, parks, monuments and wildlife refuges, an area larger than Texas. Timber companies, ranchers and many Western senators said the government was locking up land that families could have farmed and mills could have cut. Pinchot answered that unmanaged cutting would leave bare hills, floods and no timber at all within a generation.
look.prompt: What would you want to know to judge whether Roosevelt made the right trade between use now and use later?

check.q: What was new about how Roosevelt handled the 1902 coal strike?
choices: He sent troops to arrest the miners
He treated the union as an equal party and forced the owners to accept arbitration
He nationalized the coal mines
He let the strike continue through the winter
check.why: Roosevelt brought both sides to the White House and threatened to seize the mines, forcing a settlement.

check.q: How did Roosevelt distinguish between trusts?
choices: By their size only
By whether they were in railroads
Between those that were efficient and behaved and those that cheated the public
Between American and foreign owners
check.why: He believed bigness could be good if regulated, and used the Sherman Act against companies he judged harmful.

check.q: What was the disagreement between Gifford Pinchot and John Muir?
choices: Whether forests should exist
Whether Roosevelt should be president
Whether to sell public land to railroads
Whether nature should be managed for use or left as untouched wilderness
check.why: Pinchot favored scientific management for long-term use; Muir wanted wild places preserved as they were.

lessons.title: Taft, Wilson and the Election of 1912
lessons.mainIdea: The 1912 election split the Republicans and put Woodrow Wilson in office, and together the three presidents remade the Constitution, the banking system and the tax code.
reading: William Howard Taft, Roosevelt's chosen successor in 1908, was a judge by temperament who moved carefully and disliked conflict. His administration actually brought more antitrust suits than Roosevelt's, including one against U.S. Steel that Roosevelt took as a personal insult. But Taft sided with conservatives on tariffs and fired Pinchot in a dispute over Alaska coal lands. Roosevelt came home from an African safari convinced his friend had betrayed the cause and challenged him for the Republican nomination in 1912.

When party bosses gave Taft the nomination, Roosevelt walked out and formed the Progressive Party, nicknamed the Bull Moose Party after he said he felt as strong as one. Its platform called for women's suffrage, an end to child labor, workers' compensation and a national health service. The split handed the election to the Democrat, Woodrow Wilson, a former Princeton president and New Jersey governor, who won with about forty-two percent of the vote. Eugene Debs, running as a Socialist, took about six percent, nearly a million votes, the party's high point.

Wilson called his program the New Freedom and moved fast. In 1913 the *Sixteenth Amendment* allowed a federal *income tax*, and the *Seventeenth Amendment* required that senators be elected by the people rather than chosen by state legislatures, two old Populist demands. The Underwood Tariff cut import duties and used the new income tax to replace the lost revenue. Then came the *Federal Reserve Act* of 1913, which created a central banking system with twelve regional banks, including one in Chicago, able to expand or tighten the money supply and lend to banks in a panic.

In 1914 Wilson signed the Clayton Antitrust Act, which strengthened the Sherman Act and declared that labor unions were not illegal conspiracies, and created the Federal Trade Commission to police unfair business practices. On race, Wilson moved backward: his administration segregated federal offices in Washington, and he praised a film glorifying the Ku Klux Klan. Progressivism could include the reformer and the segregationist in the same person, a fact students of the era cannot avoid.

words.d: the Progressive Party Roosevelt formed in 1912 after losing the Republican nomination
the 1913 amendment allowing Congress to collect a federal income tax
the 1913 amendment providing for direct election of U.S. senators by voters
the central banking system created in 1913 to manage the money supply and support banks in a crisis
a tax on what people and businesses earn, graduated so higher incomes pay a higher rate

look.title: The Four-Way Election of 1912
look.prompt: Add up the votes for the three candidates who called themselves reformers. What does that total say about what most Americans wanted in 1912, even though the winner had a minority?

check.q: Why did Roosevelt turn against Taft?
choices: Taft sided with conservatives on tariffs, fired Pinchot and sued U.S. Steel
Taft refused to run for president
Taft supported women's suffrage
Taft abolished the Forest Service
check.why: Roosevelt saw Taft's tariff stance, the Pinchot firing and the U.S. Steel suit as betrayals of his program.

check.q: What did the Seventeenth Amendment change?
choices: It created the income tax
It required senators to be elected directly by voters instead of by state legislatures
It gave women the vote
It banned alcohol
check.why: Direct election of senators was a long-standing Populist demand adopted in 1913.

check.q: What was the main purpose of the Federal Reserve Act of 1913?
choices: To collect income taxes
To break up trusts
To create a central bank able to manage the money supply and lend to banks in a panic
To insure bank deposits
check.why: The Federal Reserve's regional banks could expand or tighten credit and support banks during crises like 1893 and 1907.

lessons.title: A Splendid Little War
lessons.mainIdea: In 1898 the United States went to war with Spain over Cuba and, in ten weeks, became an overseas power with colonies in the Caribbean and the Pacific.
reading: Cuba, ninety miles from Florida, had been fighting for independence from Spain since 1895. Spanish forces herded villagers into camps where tens of thousands died of hunger and disease. American newspapers, especially those of William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer competing for readers in New York, printed lurid stories, some true and some invented, in a style critics called *yellow journalism*. Americans who owned Cuban sugar plantations wanted stability; others wanted a fight; many simply pitied the Cubans.

On February 15, 1898, the battleship USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor, killing about 260 sailors. The cause was never proven and was probably an accident in the coal bunkers, but the press blamed Spain. Congress declared war in April. The fighting lasted about ten weeks. Commodore George Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay in the Philippines in a morning. In Cuba, Roosevelt's volunteer Rough Riders and the Black soldiers of the Ninth and Tenth Cavalry took the heights above Santiago. About 2,400 Americans died, most of them from disease, not combat.

In the Treaty of Paris, signed in December 1898, Spain gave up Cuba and handed Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, which paid 20 million dollars for the Philippines. Hawaii had been annexed that summer, five years after American planters overthrew its queen. Cuba became independent in name, but the Platt Amendment of 1901, written into Cuba's constitution under pressure, gave the United States the right to intervene and a naval base at Guantanamo Bay that it still holds.

Secretary of State John Hay called it a splendid little war, and for a time it was popular. Supporters argued that the country needed markets, coaling stations for its navy and a place among the great powers, and that Americans had a duty to bring civilization to peoples they judged unready to govern themselves. Others, including Mark Twain, Jane Addams, Andrew Carnegie and Samuel Gompers, founded the Anti-Imperialist League, arguing that a republic born in revolt against an empire could not become one without betraying its own founding. The Philippines would test that argument.

words.d: sensational, exaggerated news reporting meant to sell papers, common in the 1890s
the American battleship that exploded in Havana harbor in 1898, helping push the country into war
the 1901 terms that let the United States intervene in Cuba and keep a base at Guantanamo Bay
a policy of taking control of other lands and peoples, by conquest or by economic power

look.title: Why Fight Spain?
look.text: Four Americans in April 1898. A Hearst reporter wants a war that sells papers. A Kansas farmer's son wants adventure and has read about starving Cuban children. A New York banker wants Cuban sugar safe and Asian markets open. A Black soldier in the Tenth Cavalry wants to prove that his people can serve, in a country that lynches them.
look.prompt: Each of these people supported the war for a different reason. Which reasons do you think the government actually acted on, and how could a historian tell?

check.q: What do historians now think most likely caused the explosion of the USS Maine?
choices: A Spanish mine
A Cuban rebel attack
A German submarine
An accident, probably in the ship's coal bunkers
check.why: No proof of Spanish involvement was ever found; an internal accident is the most accepted explanation.

check.q: What did the United States gain in the Treaty of Paris of 1898?
choices: Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, plus control over Cuba
Hawaii and Alaska
Mexico's northern states
Canada's Pacific coast
check.why: Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last for a 20 million dollar payment.

check.q: What was the Anti-Imperialist League's main argument?
choices: The war cost too much money
A republic founded against empire could not rule colonies without betraying its principles
Spain should keep the Philippines
The navy was too small to hold colonies
check.why: Twain, Addams, Carnegie and others argued that ruling other peoples without their consent contradicted the Declaration of Independence.

lessons.title: The Philippines and the Debate Over Empire
lessons.mainIdea: Filipinos who had fought Spain for independence fought the United States for three more years, in a war that killed far more people than the war with Spain and split American opinion.
reading: When Dewey's ships arrived at Manila in 1898, Filipino rebels under Emilio Aguinaldo had already been fighting Spain for two years. They believed the Americans had come to help them win independence, and in June 1898 they declared a Philippine republic. President McKinley decided otherwise. He later said he had concluded that the Filipinos were unfit for self-government and that the United States must take the islands and uplift and civilize them. Most Filipinos were already Catholic and had a written constitution.

Fighting between American and Filipino forces began in February 1899, two days before the Senate ratified the treaty. The *Philippine-American War* lasted officially until 1902 and in some regions for years longer. It became a guerrilla war, and both sides committed atrocities. American troops burned villages, used a torture called the water cure and, in the province of Samar, were ordered to make the interior a howling wilderness. More than four thousand American soldiers died. Filipino deaths are harder to count; standard estimates run to roughly 200,000 or more, most of them civilians who died of famine and disease.

At home the war forced a debate the country had avoided. Senator Albert Beveridge of Indiana argued that God had made Americans the master organizers of the world and that the Philippines were the door to China's markets. The Anti-Imperialist League published soldiers' letters describing the burned villages. Mark Twain wrote that the flag should have its white stripes painted black and the stars replaced with a skull and crossbones. The Supreme Court ruled in the Insular Cases of 1901 that the Constitution did not fully follow the flag, so people in the new territories were subject to American rule without American rights.

The United States built roads, schools and a public health system in the Philippines, and Filipino elites gradually took over local government. The islands became independent in 1946. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory whose residents are citizens but cannot vote for president, a status still debated. The question of 1899, whether a democracy can rule people who did not choose it, did not go away with the empire; it returned in every later argument about American power abroad.

words.d: the war from 1899 to about 1902 in which the United States defeated Filipinos fighting for independence
a war fought by small irregular forces using ambush and hiding among the population
Supreme Court rulings from 1901 holding that full constitutional rights did not automatically extend to new territories
the right of a people to rule themselves through leaders they choose

look.title: The President Explains
look.text: McKinley told a group of visiting ministers that he had walked the White House floor night after night and prayed, and had concluded that the United States could not give the islands back to Spain, could not hand them to a rival power, and could not leave them to Filipinos he believed unfit for self-rule, so there was nothing left but to take them all and educate and uplift the people.
look.cite: William McKinley, as reported in a church magazine, 1903 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: McKinley lists three options he rejected. What fourth option is missing from his list, and why do you think he left it out?

check.q: Why did Filipino rebels feel betrayed by the United States in 1898 and 1899?
choices: The Americans gave the islands back to Spain
The Americans refused to fight Spain
They had fought Spain for independence and expected American help, but the United States took the islands instead
The Americans sided with Japan
check.why: Aguinaldo's forces had declared a republic and expected recognition; instead the United States annexed the Philippines.

check.q: How did the human cost of the Philippine-American War compare with the war against Spain?
choices: It was smaller on both sides
It was similar for Americans and smaller for Filipinos
It was fought entirely at sea
It was far larger, with thousands of American and roughly 200,000 or more Filipino deaths, mostly civilians
check.why: The guerrilla war lasted years and its famine and disease killed far more people than the ten-week war with Spain.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Insular Cases?
choices: Full constitutional rights did not automatically extend to the new territories
The Philippines were a state
The war was unconstitutional
Filipinos were U.S. citizens
check.why: The Court held that the Constitution did not fully follow the flag, allowing rule without full rights.

lessons.title: Cutting the Isthmus
lessons.mainIdea: Roosevelt got the Panama Canal built by backing a revolt against Colombia, and American doctors and West Indian laborers made the impossible dig possible.
reading: In 1898 the battleship Oregon steamed from San Francisco around the tip of South America to join the war in Cuba, a trip of about 12,000 miles that took more than two months. A canal across the narrow *isthmus* of Panama would cut the voyage to about 4,000 miles. A French company had tried in the 1880s and failed, defeated by mudslides and by yellow fever and malaria that killed thousands of workers. Roosevelt wanted the canal for the navy and for trade, and he wanted it fast.

Panama belonged to Colombia, and in 1903 Colombia's senate rejected the treaty the United States offered. Roosevelt was furious. That November, Panamanian leaders, working with the French company's agent, declared independence. An American warship stood off the coast and prevented Colombian troops from landing. Within days the United States recognized Panama and signed a treaty giving it a ten-mile-wide Canal Zone forever, for 10 million dollars and rent. Roosevelt later said he took the canal and let Congress debate. Many Latin Americans have never forgotten it.

The dig itself began in 1904. The first task was medical. Dr. William Gorgas, who had helped rid Havana of yellow fever, had learned that mosquitoes carried both yellow fever and malaria. His crews drained swamps, screened windows, sprayed oil on standing water and fumigated houses. Yellow fever vanished from the Canal Zone within two years. The engineering plan changed from a sea-level ditch to a system of locks and a huge artificial lake, which meant damming a river and lifting ships eighty-five feet.

Most of the labor was done by tens of thousands of workers from the West Indies, especially Barbados and Jamaica, who were paid in silver while white American employees were paid in gold, ate in separate mess halls and lived in separate housing. Roughly 5,600 workers died during the American construction, most of them West Indian, from disease and accidents. The canal opened in August 1914, the same month the First World War began in Europe. The United States kept the Canal Zone until a treaty signed in 1977 returned it to Panama in stages, completed at the end of 1999.

words.d: a narrow strip of land connecting two larger land masses, with water on both sides
the ten-mile-wide strip across Panama that the United States controlled from 1903 to 1999
a deadly disease spread by mosquitoes that defeated the French canal effort
a chamber with gates that raises or lowers ships between different water levels

look.title: The Voyage From New York to San Francisco
look.prompt: How much of the voyage did the canal remove? Who gained most from that saving, and who paid for it?

check.q: How did the United States gain the right to build in Panama?
choices: Colombia agreed to sell the land
It supported a Panamanian revolt against Colombia and signed a treaty with the new country
Spain ceded it in 1898
France gave up its concession for free
check.why: After Colombia rejected the treaty, an American warship blocked Colombian troops while Panama declared independence.

check.q: What was the key medical discovery that made the canal possible?
choices: A vaccine for malaria
Boiling drinking water
That mosquitoes spread yellow fever and malaria, so controlling them controlled the diseases
That the diseases came from bad air
check.why: Gorgas's mosquito control drained swamps and screened housing, ending yellow fever in the zone within two years.

choices: Most workers were Americans paid in gold
Workers were all paid equally
Few workers died because of good medical care

lessons.title: The Great Migration Comes to Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: During the First World War hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners moved north for jobs and freedom, and Chicago became a capital of Black America.
reading: In the spring of 1917 a young man in Mississippi reads a copy of the Chicago Defender that came north-to-south in a Pullman porter's bag. It tells of jobs in the stockyards at wages three times what he earns picking cotton, of schools his children could attend all year and of a city where he can vote. He and thousands like him board the Illinois Central Railroad, whose tracks run straight from New Orleans to Chicago's Twelfth Street Station. The Defender, founded by Robert Abbott in 1905, called it the Great Northern Drive.

The *Great Migration* had pushes and pulls. In the South, the boll weevil was destroying cotton, floods drowned farms and lynching went on unchecked. In the North, the war in Europe had cut off immigration, and factories making steel, meat and munitions for the Allies needed workers. Between about 1916 and 1920, roughly 500,000 Black Southerners moved north. Chicago's Black population grew from about 44,000 in 1910 to about 109,000 in 1920, and kept rising. Most settled in a narrow strip on the South Side that came to be called the Black Belt and later Bronzeville.

The migrants built institutions fast: churches like Olivet Baptist, which became one of the largest congregations in the country; the Defender itself; banks, insurance companies and the Wabash Avenue YMCA. Musicians from New Orleans brought jazz up the same railroad. In 1928 the district elected Oscar De Priest, the first Black congressman from the North. Black women who had been maids in Mississippi worked in packinghouses and garment shops for cash wages.

The North was not the promised land the Defender described. Landlords charged Black families more for worse housing and white property owners signed *restrictive covenants* promising never to sell to them, so the Black Belt grew more crowded rather than larger. White unions were often hostile, and packers used Black workers as strikebreakers, deepening the resentment. The migrants had come for freedom and found a different, less official kind of segregation. In the summer of 1919 those pressures exploded.

words.d: the movement of millions of Black Americans from the rural South to Northern and Western cities, beginning about 1916
the Black newspaper founded in 1905 that urged Southerners to come north
the South Side Chicago neighborhood that became the center of Black business, music and politics
a clause in a property deed forbidding sale or rental to people of a certain race

look.title: Black Population of Chicago
look.prompt: The population more than doubled in the 1910s, but the neighborhood boundaries barely moved. What would that mean for rents, schools and daily life?

check.q: Which was a pull factor drawing Black Southerners to Chicago during the First World War?
choices: Factory jobs opened when the war cut off European immigration
Cheap farmland in Illinois
Free railroad tickets from the government
The end of segregation in the North
check.why: War production and the halt in immigration created labor shortages that Northern employers filled with Southern migrants.

check.q: What role did the Chicago Defender play in the migration?
choices: It warned people to stay in the South
It spread news of Northern jobs and freedoms across the South and urged people to come
It was the packers' hiring office
It was a Southern white newspaper
check.why: Abbott's paper, carried south by Pullman porters, was the migration's most powerful advertisement.

check.q: Why did Chicago's Black neighborhood become more crowded instead of larger as people arrived?
choices: Migrants preferred small apartments
The city had no empty land
Restrictive covenants and hostile landlords kept Black families from moving into other areas
The Illinois Central owned the surrounding land
check.why: Deed restrictions and discrimination confined newcomers to the existing Black Belt, driving up rents and crowding.

lessons.title: Over There: America in the War
lessons.mainIdea: The United States stayed out of the First World War for nearly three years, then sent two million soldiers to France and helped decide the outcome in 1918.
reading: When war broke out in Europe in August 1914, President Wilson asked Americans to be neutral in thought as well as deed. It was hard. Many Americans had roots in Germany or Ireland and disliked Britain; more traded with Britain and France and lent them money. In May 1915 a German submarine sank the British liner Lusitania, killing about 1,200 people, including 128 Americans. Germany backed off from unrestricted submarine warfare for a time. Wilson won reelection in 1916 with the slogan that he kept us out of war.

In early 1917 Germany gambled: it resumed sinking all ships heading for Britain, betting it could starve Britain before America could act. The British then handed Wilson an intercepted telegram in which Germany's foreign secretary, Zimmermann, offered Mexico help in recovering Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined a war against the United States. On April 2, 1917, Wilson asked Congress to declare war, saying the world must be made safe for democracy. Six senators and fifty representatives voted no, including Jeannette Rankin of Montana, the first woman in Congress.

The army had about 130,000 men; it would need millions. The Selective Service Act of 1917 registered about 24 million men and drafted nearly three million. The American Expeditionary Force under General John Pershing began arriving in France in the summer of 1917, and by the autumn of 1918 about two million American soldiers were there, including some 370,000 Black troops, most assigned to labor units, though the all-Black 369th Infantry, the Harlem Hellfighters, spent longer under fire than any other American regiment. Illinois's own Black regiment, the 8th Illinois, fought as the 370th Infantry in France.

The Americans arrived as Germany made its last great offensive in the spring of 1918. Fresh troops at Belleau Wood and along the Marne helped stop it, and in the autumn more than a million Americans fought through the Meuse-Argonne forest in the war's largest American battle. Germany asked for peace, and the fighting stopped at eleven in the morning on November 11, 1918. About 116,000 Americans died in the war, roughly half of them from disease, especially the influenza pandemic of 1918 that killed some 675,000 Americans at home and abroad.

words.d: the policy of taking no side in a war
the 1917 German message offering Mexico an alliance against the United States, which helped push America into war
the system of military draft created in 1917
the U.S. Army sent to France under General Pershing in 1917 and 1918
an agreement to stop fighting; the First World War's took effect on November 11, 1918

look.title: Asking for War

look.prompt: A Black soldier from Chicago, or a Filipino, might have asked whose democracy Wilson meant. How could the same words sound inspiring to some listeners and hollow to others?

choices: The sinking of the Maine and the Panama revolt
The Lusitania sinking and Wilson's reelection

check.why: Germany's decision to sink all ships bound for Britain and its offer to Mexico turned American opinion decisively.

check.q: How did the United States raise an army of millions in 1917?
choices: Through a draft under the Selective Service Act
By hiring foreign soldiers
By relying only on volunteers

check.why: The draft registered about 24 million men and inducted nearly three million.

check.q: What accounted for roughly half of American deaths in the war?
choices: Submarine attacks
Disease, especially the 1918 influenza pandemic
Artillery at the Meuse-Argonne
Accidents in training camps
check.why: Of about 116,000 American dead, roughly half died of illness, a large share from influenza.

lessons.title: The War at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Fighting the war meant organizing the whole economy and selling the war to the public, and the government's campaign against dissent tested the meaning of free speech.
reading: Wars are won with factories as much as with soldiers. The War Industries Board, run by financier Bernard Baruch, told companies what to make and set prices; the Food Administration under Herbert Hoover persuaded families to eat less wheat and meat with slogans rather than rationing. Some 20 million Americans bought Liberty Bonds to lend the government money. With millions of men in uniform, about a million women took jobs in munitions plants, railroads and offices, and the argument that women were doing their part helped win the suffrage amendment.

The government also sold the war. The Committee on Public Information, led by journalist George Creel, produced posters, films and 75,000 volunteer speakers, the Four Minute Men, who gave short patriotic talks in theaters. The campaign fed suspicion of anything German. Schools dropped German classes, orchestras stopped playing Beethoven and sauerkraut was renamed liberty cabbage. In Collinsville, Illinois, in April 1918 a mob lynched a German-born coal miner named Robert Prager; the men tried for it were acquitted in less than an hour.

Congress passed the *Espionage Act* in 1917 and the *Sedition Act* in 1918, which made it a crime to say anything disloyal about the government, the flag or the military. About two thousand people were prosecuted. Eugene Debs, then sixty-two, gave a speech in Canton, Ohio, in June 1918 saying the working class had always fought the wars while the master class declared them. He got ten years in prison and ran for president from his cell in 1920, winning over 900,000 votes.

In Schenck v. United States (1919), the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the conviction of a socialist who had mailed leaflets urging draftees to resist. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that speech could be punished when it created a *clear and present danger*, and added that even free speech would not protect a man who falsely shouted fire in a theater. Within months Holmes began to doubt his own rule and started writing dissents that argued for broad protection of dissent. Those dissents, not the Schenck ruling, became the law of free speech decades later.

words.d: the 1917 law punishing interference with the military and the draft, still in force today
the 1918 law, repealed in 1920, that made disloyal speech about the government a crime
the test Justice Holmes set in 1919 for when the government may punish speech
a government bond sold to the public to pay for the First World War
information, often one-sided, spread to shape public opinion

look.title: The Test for Speech
look.text: The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent.
look.cite: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, opinion of the Court, Schenck v. United States, 1919
look.prompt: Apply the test to Debs's Canton speech. Was there a clear and present danger, and who decides what counts as one during a war?

Through Liberty Bonds, a War Industries Board setting production and prices, and voluntary food conservation
Through a national lottery
check.why: Bonds raised money, the WIB directed industry and Hoover's Food Administration relied on persuasion.

choices: He was elected to Congress
He fled to Canada

check.why: Debs received a ten-year sentence and still won over 900,000 votes in 1920 as a prisoner.

check.q: Why do Holmes's later dissents matter more than the Schenck ruling itself?
choices: They became the basis of modern free-speech law, which protects far more dissent than Schenck allowed
They overturned the Espionage Act
They ended the war

check.why: Holmes's shift toward broad protection of speech shaped how the Court read the First Amendment in later decades.

lessons.title: Red Summer and the Vote
lessons.mainIdea: In 1919 a stone thrown at a Chicago beach set off a week of racial violence that exposed the limits of the migration's promise, even as women finally won the vote nationwide.
reading: On Sunday, July 27, 1919, a seventeen-year-old named Eugene Williams was floating on a railroad tie off the 29th Street beach on Chicago's South Side. The beach had no legal color line but an understood one, and his raft drifted across it. White bathers threw stones; Williams went under and drowned. A white police officer refused to arrest the man witnesses pointed to. Fighting broke out on the beach and spread through the South Side by nightfall.

For seven days white gangs, many of them organized athletic clubs from the neighborhoods near the stockyards, attacked Black workers on streetcars and pulled them from their homes, and Black residents fought back and, in some cases, attacked whites who entered the Black Belt. By the time the state militia restored order, 38 people were dead, 23 Black and 15 white, more than 500 were injured and about a thousand families, mostly Black, had lost their homes to fire. Chicago's was the worst of some two dozen outbreaks that summer, from Washington to Omaha to Elaine, Arkansas, in what the writer James Weldon Johnson called the *Red Summer*.

Illinois responded with something rare: an investigation. Governor Frank Lowden appointed the Chicago Commission on Race Relations, six Black and six white members, which spent two years studying housing, jobs, policing and the press. Its 1922 report, The Negro in Chicago, found that the riot grew out of competition for housing and work, hostile policing and newspapers that printed rumors. It recommended equal treatment and open housing. Most of its recommendations were ignored for decades, but its method, evidence before judgment, was the Progressive method applied to race.

Thirteen months after the beach, on August 26, 1920, the *Nineteenth Amendment* became law and about 26 million women became eligible to vote. Two decades of reform had produced the income tax, the Federal Reserve, food safety, the direct election of senators, national forests and the largest expansion of the vote in the country's history. It had also produced an empire, a wartime attack on free speech and a color line the reformers had mostly left alone. The next chapter picks up the story in a country that was about to try to forget all of it for a decade.

words.d: the wave of racial violence that struck more than two dozen American cities and towns in 1919
a period of mass violence between racial groups, in 1919 usually begun by white attacks on Black residents
the biracial body appointed by Illinois's governor to investigate the 1919 riot
all the people who are eligible to vote
